L37@P3: Reports on Computer Systems Technology
L38@P3: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology
L39@P3: (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the nation’s
L40@P3: measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of
L41@P3: concept implementations, and technical analysis to advance the development and productive use of
L42@P3: information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of technical, physical,
L43@P3: administrative, and management standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of
L44@P3: sensitive unclassified information in federal computer systems. This Special Publication 800-series
L45@P3: reports on ITL’s research, guidance, and outreach efforts in computer security and its collaborative
L46@P3: activities with industry, government, and academic organizations.

L50@P4: furtherance of its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act
L51@P4: (FISMA) of 2002, Public Law 107-347.

L53@P4: providing adequate information security for all agency operations and assets, but such standards and

L71@P5: Compliance with NIST Standards and Guidelines
L72@P5: NIST develops and issues standards, guidelines, and other publications to assist federal agencies in
L73@P5: implementing the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) of 2002 and in managing costeffective programs to protect their information and information systems.
L74@P5: • Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are developed by NIST in accordance with
L75@P5: FISMA. FIPS are approved by the Secretary of Commerce and are compulsory and binding for
L76@P5: federal agencies. Since FISMA requires that federal agencies comply with these standards,
L77@P5: agencies may not waive their use.
L78@P5: • Guidance documents and recommendations are issued in the NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-
L79@P5: series. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) policies (including OMB FISMA Reporting
L80@P5: Instructions for the Federal Information Security Management Act and Agency Privacy
L81@P5: Management) state that, for other than national security programs and systems, agencies must
L82@P5: follow NIST guidance.1
L83@P5: • Other security-related publications, including NIST interagency and internal reports (NISTIRs)
L84@P5: and ITL Bulletins, provide technical and other information about NIST’s activities. These
L85@P5: publications are mandatory only when so specified by OMB.
L86@P5: 
L87@P5: 1
L88@P5:  While agencies are required to follow NIST guidance in accordance with OMB policy, there is flexibility within NIST’s
L89@P5: guidance in how agencies apply the guidance. Unless otherwise specified by OMB, the 800-series guidance documents
L90@P5: published by NIST generally allow agencies some latitude in the application. Consequently, the application of NIST guidance
L91@P5: by agencies can result in different security solutions that are equally acceptable, compliant with the guidance, and meet the
L92@P5: OMB definition of adequate security for federal information systems. When assessing federal agency compliance with NIST
L93@P5: guidance, auditors, evaluators, and assessors should consider the intent of the security concepts and principles articulated
L94@P5: within the particular guidance document and how the agency applied the guidance in the context of its specific mission
L95@P5: responsibilities, operational environments, and unique organizational conditions.

L79@P3: Abstract
L80@P3: In light of an increasing number of cybersecurity events, organizations can improve resilience by
L81@P3: ensuring that their risk management processes include comprehensive recovery planning.
L82@P3: Identifying and prioritizing organization resources helps to guide effective plans and realistic test
L83@P3: scenarios. This preparation enables rapid recovery from incidents when they occur and helps to
L84@P3: minimize the impact on the organization and its constituents. Additionally, continually
L85@P3: improving recovery planning by learning lessons from past events, including those of other
L86@P3: organizations, helps to ensure the continuity of important mission functions. This publication
L87@P3: provides tactical and strategic guidance regarding the planning, playbook developing, testing,
L88@P3: and improvement of recovery planning. It also provides an example scenario that demonstrates
L89@P3: guidance and informative metrics that may be helpful for improving resilience of information
L90@P3: systems.

L169@P7: Executive Summary
L170@P7: The number of major cyber events continues to increase sharply every year, taking advantage of
L171@P7: weaknesses in processes and people as well as technologies.1 There has been widespread recognition that
L172@P7: some of these cybersecurity (cyber) events cannot be stopped and solely focusing on preventing cyber
L173@P7: events from occurring is a flawed approach. Organizations should improve their prevention capabilities
L174@P7: with modern technology and tools while augmenting their cyber event detection and response capabilities.
L175@P7: In 2015, members of the Federal Government reviewed cybersecurity capabilities and, as documented in
L176@P7: the Cybersecurity Strategy and Implementation Plan (CSIP) [2], identified significant inconsistencies in
L177@P7: cyber event response capabilities among federal agencies. The CSIP stated that agencies must improve
L178@P7: their response capabilities. Although there are existing federal policies, standards, and guidelines on cyber
L179@P7: event handling, none of them focuses solely on improving cybersecurity recovery capabilities, and the
L180@P7: fundamental information is not captured in a single document. The previous recovery content tends to be
L181@P7: spread out in documents such as security, contingency, disaster recovery, and business continuity plans.
L182@P7: Recovery is one part of the enterprise risk management process lifecycle; for example, the Framework for
L183@P7: Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity [3], better known as the Cybersecurity Framework
L184@P7: (CSF), defines five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.2 These functions are all
L185@P7: critical for a complete defense. At a more fundamental level, the capabilities in the Recover function have
L186@P7: a significant effect across the organization by providing realistic data for improving other capabilities.
L187@P7: Recovery can be described in two phases focused on separate tactical and strategic outcomes. The
L188@P7: immediate tactical recovery phase is largely achieved through the execution of the recovery playbook
L189@P7: planned prior to the incident (with input from Detect and other CSF functions as required). The second
L190@P7: phase is more strategic, and it focuses on the continuous improvement of all the CSF functions to mitigate
L191@P7: the likelihood and impact of future incidents (based on the lessons learned from the incident as well as
L192@P7: from other organization and industry practices).
L193@P7: This document is not an operational playbook; it provides guidance to help organizations plan and prepare
L194@P7: recovery from a cyber event and integrate the processes and procedures into their enterprise risk
L195@P7: management plans. This document is not intended to be used by organizations responding to an active
L196@P7: cyber event, but as a guide to develop recovery plans in the form of customized playbooks. As referred to
L197@P7: in this document, a playbook is an action plan that documents an actionable set of steps an organization
L198@P7: can follow to successfully recover from a cyber event. While many fundamental activities are similar for
L199@P7: organizations of different sizes and from different industry sectors, each playbook can focus on a unique
